concept.title: Testing plug-ins
concept.shortdesc: A plug-in changes how DITA-OT processes content, so a change that looks correct on its own can break the output. Testing a plug-in means installing it into a clean DITA-OT installation, running its transformations on known test content, and checking the results.

conbody.p: Plug-ins depend on parts of DITA-OT that change between releases, such as XSLT templates, Ant targets, parameters and extension points. Tests that run the plug-in in a real DITA-OT installation find these problems before your users do, and make it safer to change the plug-in or move it to a new DITA-OT release.

section.title: Organizing a plug-in project
section.p: Keep the plug-in, its test content and its build files in one source repository, but package and install only the plug-in files. A project for a plug-in that adds an HTML5-based transformation type can look like this:
section.codeblock: dita-ot-gradle-plugin ├── plugin.xml Plug-in configuration file ├── build_sample-html5.xml Ant script for the transformation type ├── css │ └── sample.css Resources used by the plug-in ├── test-content Test maps and topics │ ├── sample.ditamap │ └── topics │ ├── intro.dita │ └── usage.dita ├── build.gradle.kts Build script that installs and tests the plug-in ├── settings.gradle.kts ├── gradle.properties ├── gradlew ├── gradlew.bat ├── gradle │ └── wrapper └── ci └── dita-ot-matrix.yml Continuous integration workflow
section.p: The files fall into three groups:

dlentry.dd: The plugin.xml file and the files it refers to, such as Ant scripts, XSLT stylesheets, CSS and language files. These are the only files in the plug-in ZIP file that users install. See .
DITA maps and topics that exercise the features of the plug-in. They stay in the repository and are not installed.
Scripts that download DITA-OT, install the plug-in, run the tests, and run them again in continuous integration (CI). The example above uses a build, described in .

section.p: This layout follows the advice in to store plug-in source code outside the DITA-OT installation directory.

section.title: Levels of testing
section.p: A plug-in test strategy usually covers three levels. Each level rules out a cause of failure before you look at the next one.

dlentry.dd: Confirm that the test content is valid DITA, so that a failure points to the plug-in and not to the content. Use the dita validate subcommand described in .
Confirm that the plug-in installs into a clean DITA-OT installation, as described in , and that its transformation type appears in the output of dita transtypes.
Run the plug-in's transformation on the test content and check the result. Most regressions appear at this level.

section.title: Choosing test content
section.p: Cover the cases that your plug-in handles, for example:

ul.li: A simple map with a few topics
Cross-references, key references and content references
Conditional processing with a DITAVAL file
Special characters, and empty or optional elements

section.p: A small set of maps under version control gives you a regression suite that is easy to run and to diagnose.

section.title: Testing from the command line
section.p: To test a plug-in by hand, install it and run its transformation with the dita command:
Use --filter to apply a DITAVAL file, and --verbose or --debug to get more detail when a test fails.

section.title: Checking the output
section.p: A transformation that finishes without errors does not prove that the output is correct. Check the result, for example by:

ul.li: Confirming that the expected files exist
Checking that generated XML or HTML is well-formed
Comparing the output with a known-good baseline and reviewing the differences
Checking links in the content and in the generated output

section.title: Automating tests
section.p: Manual tests are easy to skip. A build tool can run the install, validate, transform and check steps with one command, on every change. shows a complete example that uses Gradle.
Run the same tests against each DITA-OT version that your plug-in supports. A plug-in that works on one release can fail on another when core templates or parameters change. See .
